stories.summary: Image source, Eagan Salla/BBC Image caption, Tundu Lissu says the trial is politically motivated By Wycliffe Muia Â and Â Alfred Lasteck ,Â BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Dar es Salaam Published 6 November 2026, 09:33 GMT Updated 1 hour ago Tanzania's main opposition leader, Tundu Lissu, has been found guilty of inciting unrest and sentenced to four years in jail, in a case that has raised concerns about political freedom in the East African country. A panel of three judges at the High Court in Dar es Salaam acquitted him of the more serious offence of treason, saying prosecutors had failed to prove a key element of that charge. But they said the 58-year-old, who has been detained since April last year, had encouraged his supporters to disrupt the disputed 2025 general election. Lissu, who leads the opposition Chadema party, has denied the charges, describing the prosecution as politically motivated. The court said his campaign slogan "No Reforms, No Election" was sufficient for him to be convicted of the charge of incitement. "By uttering those words with the intention of disseminating them to the public, the accused incited the public to disrupt the 2025 elections," the court ruled.

Ces départs massifs interviennent après les mesures prises le 2 novembre par les autorités guinéennes pour mettre fin à l’orpaillage illégal. stories.title: Somalia's top court rejects president's term extension amid political crisis
stories.summary: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud's four-year mandate expired in May By Wycliffe Muia Published 6 November 2026, 08:04 GMT Updated 5 hours ago Somalia's Supreme Court has ruled that President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud unlawfully extended his term, escalating a political crisis and a standoff between the presidency and judiciary. Thursday's ruling came a day after Mohamud dismissed Chief Justice Bashe Yusuf Ahmed - a move which the court said the president lacked the authority to take. The court also ordered political leaders to agree on an electoral plan within 30 days and hold elections within 90 days, potentially disrupting government plans for nationwide polls next year. Mohamud's four-year mandate expired in May, but his administration extended it by a year through law changes approved by parliament in March. Opposition groups accuse him of using the constitutional changes to prolong his rule.

Their work will contribute to the conference's scientific outputs, thematic synthesis, and official documentation. Eligibility requirement: Applicants must be based in Ethiopia and available to work on-site in Addis Ababa throughout the conference period, 23-27 November 2026 .

stories.title: Kenyan pharmacists warn against viral craze of using allergy drug for vaginal tightening
stories.summary: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Cetirizine is commonly used to relieve allergy symptoms By Wycliffe Muia Reporting from Nairobi Published 5 November 2026 Kenyan pharmacists have warned women against inserting allergy tablets into their vaginas in an attempt to make them tighter, following the spread of potentially dangerous medical advice on social media. The warning follows a wave of social media posts promoting cetirizine - a widely available oral antihistamine used to treat allergies - as a way of tightening the vagina, supposedly to enhance sexual pleasure. Although antihistamines can sometimes cause dryness as a side effect, experts say this does not strengthen vaginal muscles. "Dryness is not tightness... instead, it may increase friction, discomfort, and the risk of tissue injury," the Pharmaceutical Society of Kenya (PSK) said. "Inserting oral tablets is unsafe. Cetirizine tablets are made to be swallowed. Their ingredients have not been tested on delicate vaginal tissue," it added.

The trial was funded by the US, under Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, who has a long record of expressing scepticism about vaccines. Police have seized a batch of vaccines from the research centre at the heart of the controversy. The proposed trial drew international criticism because it planned to withhold a vaccine recommended by the World Health Organization (WHO) from half of the participating newborns. stories.title: Can an African feminist have a white wedding? It’s complicated | Patience Akumu
stories.summary: Patience and Mark at their wedding. ‘Getting married as an African feminist felt like the pope renouncing Catholicism – uncomfortable and unlikely.’ Photograph: Courtesy of Patience Akumu View image in fullscreen Patience and Mark at their wedding. ‘Getting married as an African feminist felt like the pope renouncing Catholicism – uncomfortable and unlikely.’ Photograph: Courtesy of Patience Akumu Can an African feminist have a white wedding? It’s complicated Patience Akumu I wanted to be a beacon of black feminist love; my friends and family teased me for being a sellout W e had been together 20 years, had two children and had a customary marriage with our village sub-county two years ago without any real plans for a church wedding. So we called our second ceremony a celebration of love and not a wedding. How else would a self-professed African feminist survive being the centre of a colonial and Abrahamic religious ceremony that also manages to reinforce the most male-centred aspects of African culture? Our invitations came directly from me and my partner Mark, not – as is traditional – from our families, and in the form of a playful gif featuring the song Love Potion from the South African group Mafikizolo, a reminder that this was a wedding on our terms.

stories.title: Roy Moxham obituary
stories.summary: Roy Moxham visited India many times, partly to carry out research for his books View image in fullscreen Roy Moxham visited India many times, partly to carry out research for his books Obituary Roy Moxham obituary My uncle Roy Moxham, who has died aged 86, was a former tea plantation supervisor who in later life turned his hand to writing about tea and about India , a country he visited many times on extended trips. His most successful book was The Great Hedge of India (2001), which was published not just in English but in multiple Indian languages. The hedge of the title, which was four metres high and 2.5m wide, was made of thorny shrubs and stretched 2,500 miles across British India to form a customs line guarded by 12,000 men on behalf of the East India Company. Following independence in 1947 it all but disappeared, but Roy spent many of his visits to the country looking for vestiges, eventually finding a small surviving section. He cut a branch from it, and it is now in the possession of his brother John (my father), kept safely in his study.
